html:
The Chernobyl disaster was the explosion of a nuclear reactor near the town of Pripyat in Soviet Ukraine on 26 April 1986, the worst nuclear accident in history. Reactor 4 blew up during a safety test, and the fire that followed threw radioactive material across much of Europe.

The cause was a mix of a flawed Soviet reactor design and mistakes by the staff running the test. Two workers died in the blast, and dozens of firefighters and plant staff died of radiation sickness in the months after. Pripyat, home to tens of thousands of people, was evacuated the next day, and an exclusion zone of about 30 kilometres was cleared around the plant.

At first the Soviet government said almost nothing. It admitted the accident only after workers at a nuclear plant in Sweden detected the radiation on their own clothes.

  • Cases of thyroid cancer rose sharply among children in the most contaminated areas.
  • Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and workers took part in the cleanup.
  • A concrete shelter was built over the ruin in 1986, and a vast steel arch was slid over it in 2016.

The disaster deepened distrust of the Soviet state. Mikhail Gorbachev later said it was a turning point, and perhaps a cause of the end of the Soviet Union. It also slowed the building of nuclear power plants, which run on nuclear fission, across the world. The Fukushima accident in Japan in 2011 renewed the same fears.
